research_question: Does the ratio between bottleneck width and expansion width explain the parameter-efficiency pattern observed in Experiments 005 and 006?
observations: Experiment 006 replicated h128_256 at mean Q.ANT accuracy 0.911 with 136074 parameters.
h256 reached mean Q.ANT accuracy 0.9072 with 203530 parameters.
h32_256 reached mean Q.ANT accuracy 0.8998 with 36138 parameters, close to h128 at 0.9002 with 101770 parameters.
h64_64_256 did not show a general benefit from adding depth, reaching mean Q.ANT accuracy 0.8992.
hypothesis: Parameter efficiency depends on a structured bottleneck-to-expansion ratio rather than expansion or depth alone. For at least some bottleneck widths, increasing the following layer width will improve accuracy per parameter up to a useful range, after which gains diminish.
falsification: Weaken or reject the hypothesis if expansion ratios show no repeatable relationship with accuracy/parameter efficiency across seeds, or if matched single-layer controls are consistently as efficient or more efficient.

proposed_method.analysis: Compare mean accuracy and variability across seeds, construct an accuracy-versus-parameter Pareto frontier, and examine performance as a function of expansion ratio.

limitations: This experiment remains limited to MNIST and a small training subset.
Three seeds provide replication but only a limited estimate of training variability.
Q.ANT CPU backend validates execution/correctness; it does not establish photonic latency, energy efficiency, optical noise behavior, or hardware performance.
